name: Dr. Walter Willett
who: MD, DrPH — Professor of Epidemiology and Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; ran the Nurses' Health Study and co-chaired the EAT-Lancet Commission on planetary diets.
why: The most-cited nutrition scientist alive; his cohort work and Healthy Eating Plate reshaped dietary guidelines worldwide.
reach: Public profile modest relative to output; no notable social following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Build your plate around mostly vegetables, whole grains, and healthy protein, his Healthy Eating Plate ratio.

name: Dr. Frank Hu
who: MD, PhD — Chair of the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; leads large-scale cohort research on diet, diabetes and cardiovascular risk.
why: One of the most-published nutrition epidemiologists in the world; his work underpins global diabetes-prevention guidance.
reach: Academic profile, no notable public social following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Think in long-term dietary patterns tracked over years, not single superfoods, for chronic-disease risk.

name: Dr. David Ludwig
who: MD, PhD — endocrinologist at Boston Children's Hospital/Harvard Medical School; runs an obesity-prevention clinic and developed the carbohydrate-insulin model of obesity.
why: Bridges bench research and a working clinic; his insulin-carb framework reset the low-fat-vs-low-carb debate.
reach: Modest public following; reach mainly via bestselling books (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Watch how refined carbohydrates affect your hunger and insulin, not just the calories you eat.

name: Dr. Christopher Gardner
who: PhD — Director of Nutrition Studies at the Stanford Prevention Research Center; led the landmark DIETFITS low-fat vs. low-carb trial.
why: Runs some of the most rigorous, most-cited diet-comparison trials in the field.
reach: Academic reach with occasional mainstream press, no verified following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Pick whichever sustainable diet style you can stick with — his own trial found adherence beat macros.

name: Dr. Marion Nestle
who: PhD, MPH — Paulette Goddard Professor Emerita of Nutrition, Food Studies and Public Health at NYU; author of Food Politics.
why: Defined food-industry-influence scholarship; decades of books and her Food Politics blog still set the agenda for nutrition-policy debate.
reach: Blog and book audience, moderate social following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Read a nutrition claim with an eye toward who funded the study or wrote the guideline.

name: Dr. Sarah Berry
who: PhD — Reader in Nutritional Sciences at King's College London and Chief Scientist at ZOE; leads the PREDICT population nutrition studies.
why: Her PREDICT research is the evidence base behind a personalized-nutrition program used by hundreds of thousands.
reach: Modest personal following; reach mainly via the ZOE platform and podcast (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Expect your blood-sugar response to a food to differ from everyone else's — personalize, don't generalize.

name: Dr. Federica Amati
who: Registered Nutritionist (ANutr) with a PhD — Head Nutritionist at ZOE and Clinical Lead for Nutrition at Imperial College Health Partners.
why: Translates population science into daily clinical and consumer guidance at scale; author of a bestselling nutrition-myth book.
reach: IG in the low hundreds of thousands (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Translate big population nutrition science into small, consistent daily habits rather than overhauling everything at once.

name: Tim Spector
who: MD, PhD — Professor of Genetic Epidemiology at King's College London; pivoted a career in twin and microbiome research into founding ZOE.
why: Turned twin-study and microbiome findings into the most-listened diet-science podcast and one of the largest personalized-nutrition programs in the world; nutrition is now his full-time research focus, which is why he clears the specialization gate.
reach: IG in the mid hundreds of thousands; podcast in global nutrition charts (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Track how your own blood sugar and gut respond to foods, instead of following generic rules.

name: Dr. Stacy Sims
who: PhD in Exercise Physiology and Nutrition Science — adjunct senior lecturer at the University of Waikato; consults with elite female athletes and teams.
why: Built the female-specific sports-nutrition field largely from scratch; ROAR and Next Level rewired how women train and fuel.
reach: IG in the low hundreds of thousands (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Train and fuel according to your own physiology, not a male-based default sports-nutrition template.

name: Dr. Kevin Hall
who: PhD (physics) — spent two decades as a senior investigator in NIH's metabolism and nutrition research group; retired from NIH in 2025 following a public dispute over research independence; current institutional role not independently confirmed here.
why: His controlled-feeding trials gave the first causal evidence that ultra-processed food drives overeating — the single most field-shifting nutrition experiment of the decade.
reach: Academic and media profile, no verified social following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Cut back on ultra-processed foods specifically — his controlled trials found they drive overeating on their own.

name: Dr. Gil Carvalho
who: MD, PhD (biophysics) — physician-scientist behind Nutrition Made Simple!, an evidence-review channel fact-checking nutrition claims.
why: One of the few MDs doing rigorous, citation-backed myth-busting at real scale; borderline on active clinical practice, but the education work is genuinely field-shaping.
reach: Subscriber base in the low hundreds of thousands (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Trace a bold nutrition claim back to its original citation before you believe it.

name: Dr. Alan Flanagan
who: PhD in Nutritional Sciences (University of Surrey) — Registered Associate Nutritionist running the Alinea Nutrition consultancy, specializing in circadian nutrition.
why: Rare combination of a rigorous PhD and an active client-facing practice; a leading voice against nutrition-influencer overreach.
reach: Modest following, mostly a professional/industry audience (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Pay attention to when you eat, not just what, aligning bigger meals with your active hours.

name: Dr. Michael Greger
who: MD — founder of NutritionFacts.org, the largest free video library of evidence reviews on nutrition; author of How Not to Die.
why: Borderline on current clinical practice, but the scale and rigor of his evidence-synthesis library is field-defining for plant-based nutrition education.
reach: Video and newsletter audience in the high hundreds of thousands to low millions (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Check a bold claim against a free evidence-review library before you accept it.

name: Dr. Gemma Newman
who: MBBS — practicing NHS GP in the UK ('The Plant Power Doctor') focused on lifestyle and plant-based nutrition in primary care.
why: Borderline on formal nutrition-science credentials, but an active GP practice plus consistent, credentialed public education on diet and chronic disease.
reach: IG in the tens to low hundreds of thousands (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Bring diet and lifestyle questions to your primary-care doctor, not only a specialist, for chronic disease.

name: Dr. Valter Longo
who: PhD in Biochemistry — Professor of Gerontology and Biological Sciences at USC and Director of the USC Longevity Institute; developed the Fasting-Mimicking Diet.
why: Turned lab longevity research into a clinically tested dietary intervention now used in hospitals and licensed commercially.
reach: Moderate public following, larger in Italy/Europe (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Consider periodic, clinically tested fasting-style protocols rather than improvising extended fasts on your own.

name: Prof. Susan Jebb
who: PhD — Professor of Diet and Population Health at the University of Oxford and Chair of the UK Food Standards Agency.
why: Shapes UK national nutrition and food-safety policy directly; decades advising government on obesity and diet.
reach: Academic/policy profile, minimal public social presence (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Treat national dietary guidelines as a baseline — they're built from population-level evidence.

name: Prof. Jose Ordovas
who: PhD — Director of the Nutrition and Genomics Laboratory at Tufts University's Jean Mayer USDA Human Nutrition Research Center.
why: Founding figure of nutrigenomics; his gene-diet interaction studies (e.g., Mediterranean-diet research) underlie the whole personalized-nutrition field.
takeaway: Recognize your genes can shape how you individually respond to a diet like the Mediterranean pattern.

name: Dr. Sumantra Ray
who: Physician-scientist — founder and Chair of the NNEdPro Global Institute for Food, Nutrition and Health, a WHO-collaborating nutrition-education program spanning over 100 countries.
why: Built the largest cross-border nutrition-in-medicine education network, training clinicians worldwide to actually use nutrition science.
reach: Institutional/academic reach, no personal social following (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Expect your doctor to be trained in practical nutrition, and ask about it if guidance feels thin.

name: Prof. Barbara Rolls
who: PhD — Helen A. Guthrie Chair of Nutritional Sciences at Penn State; created the Volumetrics approach to satiety and portion research.
why: Her food-volume/energy-density research reshaped how dietitians and the public think about fullness and portion control.
reach: Academic and book audience only (approx, unverified)
takeaway: Fill your plate with high-volume, low-energy-density foods like vegetables and broths to feel full on less.
